Orchot Tzadikim 19:17: The twelfth: that he remember that the Holy One, blessed be He, sees the thoughts of his heart. See how one who goes to serve before a king adorns and beautifies himself, as it is written (Esther 4:2), "for none may enter the king's gate clothed in sackcloth"; and as you see with Joseph the righteous, peace upon him (Genesis 41:14), "and Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they rushed him out of the pit, and he shaved and changed his clothes, and came before Pharaoh." And now see that there is no adornment for one who stands before a king forever, comparable to standing before the king for a single hour. If so, we who stand before the King of kings forever — for He sees the thoughts of our hearts in secret and in the open, and there is no escape from Him, for He is everywhere — must always think of His greatness, and resolve in our hearts to do His will, and adorn ourselves in our thoughts before Him.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:18: The thirteenth: that he remember that his wisdom exceeds his deeds, that he does not act according to his wisdom. And he has money, and does not do good with his money in proportion to his wealth. And let him think: who is the man who, if someone came to him and said, "you shall have a hundred gold pieces on condition that you give ten gold pieces to my friend," would refuse? How much more so should one do this before the exalted Lord! And do not say: if I had reached such-and-such wealth, or if I knew more learning than I know, I would do what I am obligated to do in service. For whoever says this speaks great vanity, for this is exactly how the evil inclination pushes a person off. Rather, every person should act at once according to his present wisdom and wealth, whatever they are now; and if he has more later, let him do more.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:19: The fourteenth: that a person remember, when he shows his fellow a pleasant countenance, how his heart is drawn to love him, as it is written (Proverbs 27:19), "as water reflects face to face, so does the heart of man to man." How much more so if he sees a king receive him with a pleasant countenance and show him that he loves him — how much he will love him, how much he will honor him and submit before him, and how much he will boast and glory in this. How much more so regarding the Blessed Creator, who has made known to us that He loves us, and has promised to love us in every generation, as it is said (Leviticus 26:44), "and yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them, nor will I loathe them, to destroy them, to break My covenant with them" — that we are obligated to love the Blessed Creator with all our heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:20: The fifteenth: that he remember that a person prepares his needs before he needs them, though he does not know whether he will live to enjoy them or not. And one who goes on a long journey — how he prepares provisions for the way! How much more so should we do this for the long world [to come], which is a long journey, when suddenly the Omnipresent sends His messenger to bring the person, whether or not he has provisions. Therefore let him be careful to have provisions ready before he sets out on his journey and before he needs them.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:21: The sixteenth: that a person remember his friends, young men and stronger than he, who enjoyed great pleasure, yet did not live long. And death does not delay in coming at any hour, and no person can control it. And let him think: the soul is a deposit in his hand, and he does not know when the owner of the deposit will come and demand it back, and he must hasten to clean the deposit, so that he return it as clean as it came into his hand.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:22: The seventeenth: that he remember a very good level — to withdraw from people when he can free himself from them, and sit alone in his room. For most transgressions are only completed by two people, such as illicit relations, slander, lies, and flattery. From all these, whoever sits alone is saved, for he does not become proud toward people, and does not listen to their mockery. And while he stands there [among people], he is obligated to rebuke them in three ways: by physical action, like Pinchas, who took a spear in his hand (Numbers 25:7); by words, as Moses our teacher, peace upon him, did, who said to the wicked man (Exodus 2:13), "why do you strike your fellow?"; and in the heart, as David said (Psalms 26:5), "I have hated the gathering of evildoers, and will not sit with the wicked." And who can quarrel with them constantly, since they are constantly transgressing? But when you sit alone, you have removed all this punishment from yourself, and you are saved from many sins. But he should associate with the pious, sit among them and learn from them, as it is written (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:23: The eighteenth: that he remember the kindnesses of the Omnipresent, who saves him from the mishaps of the world. He sees how many people die in harsh suffering: from hunger, from thirst, from deadly poisons, from leprosy, from the sword, from water, and from fire; and he knows within himself that he deserves all these troubles because of the many transgressions he has committed, not having kept God's charge. And even though he is completely wicked, the Blessed Lord had compassion on him and saved him from all these troubles. Let him know how fitting it is to submit before his Maker, and to seek forgiveness from Him each time, and to be careful in his service to praise Him, and to ask Him to guard him from all the troubles that arise in the world, as the verse says (Exodus 15:26), "and He said, if you will diligently listen to the voice of the Lord your God... none of the diseases which I have brought upon the Egyptians will I bring upon you, for I am the Lord your Healer." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 33a): it is not the venomous creature that kills, but sin that kills.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:24: The nineteenth: that he remember and consider that if he has money, it is a deposit with him, for whenever the Blessed Lord wishes, He will take it from his hand and deposit it with another. Therefore a person should not be distressed about repaying what he owes his fellow; for instance, if he stole, he should return the stolen item joyfully, and praise the exalted Lord that his hand is able to return the stolen item. And let him be careful not to fear for his money, but think: whatever the Creator wishes will happen, for everything belongs to Him. When He wishes, He places it in his hand, and when He wishes, He takes it from him. He should not despise a poor man for his poverty, nor think that his own wealth came to him by his own merit, but should think that the exalted God, in His mercy, gave it to him. And let him ask Him to give him mastery over his wealth to do the will of the exalted Creator, so that his riches not be stored up for his own harm.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:25: The twentieth: that he remember and reflect on the difference between the upper and lower worlds, and understand that he is small and lowly compared to the supernal things. And let him understand that the Holy One, blessed be He, allotted him a good portion, for He gave him dominion over the whole world: over the beasts, the wild animals, the fish, the birds, the fruits, the herbs; and made known to him the secrets of His greatness, His mighty deeds, and His wonders. And how obligated he is to thank Him for all this, like a lowly servant whom his master raised up and exalted above all his officers and servants. How much more so one who has attained knowledge of his Creator, who is the Master of masters, is obligated to humble himself before Him, and praise Him with awe and fear.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:26: The twenty-first: that he always remember all the King's commandments. And let him accustom himself to do good until he is very well accustomed to it, and afterward add still more. And let him ask God for help, that He assist him and grant him knowledge of wisdom, and strengthen his limbs to bear His commandments, and to rise from level to level.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:27: The twenty-second: that he always remember to do good with his fellows, to help them in their toil and their burden. And let him love them as he loves his own soul, and hate to do to them what he hates for himself. And let him strive to acquire faithful brothers and friends who will help him in his Torah study, for when your heart is whole with them, they will love you. Let those at peace with you be many, but reveal your secret to only one in a thousand.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:28: The twenty-third: that he always remember the greatness of the exalted God. And let him understand the creations of the world, great and small, and how the celestial spheres move, the sun and the moon and the stars, and the falling of rain and the blowing of the winds, and many more such things too numerous to recount. And because a person constantly sees these wonders, his heart is not astonished at them; but when the sun or the moon is eclipsed, then he is greatly astonished — this is because it is not constant and habitual, like the sun's circuit every day from east to west. Therefore look upon them, and make yourself as though you had never seen these wonders in all your days, and let it seem as if you had been blind until now and have just now opened your eyes — then it would seem very wondrous to you. Do this to yourself every day. And so David said (Psalms 139:14), "Your works are wondrous, and my soul knows it very well."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:29: The twenty-fourth: that he remember and think: a person with weak eyes cannot see fine, delicate engravings on vessels of silver and gold; even though he sees the vessel, he still cannot examine it as closely as one with strong eyes. So too, if he studied Torah and wisdom in his youth, and it seems to him that he understands them properly, he should not rely on that understanding, for wisdom grows stronger as one advances in years, more than what he understood in his youth. Therefore, as your wisdom grows stronger, begin to reflect on your affairs. And then you will understand and gain further insight, and grasp the clarity of the matter more than at first. And always continue to seek out from every person what you do not know, as the matter is said (Psalms 119:99), "from all my teachers I have gained understanding." And do not think: who can teach me anything new beyond what I already knew in my youth? Of this it is said (Proverbs 26:12), "you see a man wise in his own eyes — there is more hope for a fool than for him."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:30: The twenty-fifth: that he always remember the pleasantness of the World to Come. And let him remove love of this world from his heart, and strengthen love of the World to Come within him. And one of the pious already said: just as water and fire cannot be joined in one vessel, so this world and the World to Come cannot be joined in the heart of the believer. And he should love this world only insofar as he takes provisions from it for the World to Come.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:31: The twenty-sixth: that he remember those who stand in obedience to the king's command, fearful and terrified of the king's punishment. How much more so should he fear the punishment of the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and hasten to run to His service.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:32: The twenty-seventh: that he remember someone who angered the king and was sentenced to death, and the king had compassion on him and disciplined him a little instead, and restored him to his place — how glad that offender would be to bear a little suffering in place of death. And so a person, if he is suffering, should think: he transgressed the commandments of the Lord and was liable to death, and the Lord was lenient with him and brought him suffering or loss of money instead of the death he deserved. Therefore let him accept it with joy and love, and this is a good sign that he desires the decree of the Lord.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:33: The twenty-eighth: that he remember someone who gives his house to a person as an outright gift, and the recipient wishes to demolish and rebuild it according to his own judgment, and the giver cannot object because he has already relinquished it from his own hand. So a person should hand over his soul, his wife, his children, and all his money into the hand of the Blessed Lord, and let everything be given over to Him as a gift. And since he has already given himself over into the hand of the Blessed Lord from the outset, he has thereby placed his trust in the Blessed Lord, and his heart has already believed, accepting out of love whatever the Blessed Creator decrees upon him. And even if the Blessed Lord sends no evil at all — neither upon his body, nor his money, nor his children, nor his wife — nonetheless he has great reward for his proper resolve, having prepared his heart to bear everything for love of his Maker.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:34: The twenty-ninth: that he remember and reflect on people, and see that there is one person equal to a hundred, not because of his body, but because of his understanding, his wisdom, and his righteousness. Therefore hasten the improvement of your soul, for all virtues come from it. For if a person were strong, healthy, and handsome beyond compare, he would be worth nothing if he were a fool. And if a person were ugly and weak, but exceedingly wise, he would rise to greatness and importance.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:35: The thirtieth: that he remember [this]: if a person came to a foreign land, knowing no one and known by no one, and the ruler of the province took pity on him and gave him his food every day, and warned him not to rebel against him and not to transgress his commands, and made known to him a good reward for his service, and warned him about the journey [ahead] without telling him the time — truly this servant is obligated to submit and abandon pride, and inquire about the king's service, in what way he might do his will, and love a stranger like himself, and strive to increase in the service of the province, since he has no one to take pity on him. So truly is a person a stranger in the world. When the time comes for him to enter the air of the world, even if the whole world tried to hasten or delay it by a moment, or to bind one of his limbs, they could not. And likewise, after he enters the air of the world, the whole world could not give him sustenance except the Faithful God. And he is like one alone with no companion, and like a stranger with no acquaintance except his Master, and with no one to take pity on him but his Creator.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:36: Behold, we have completed thirty things that a person should always remember. We have mentioned them briefly, and let each person add depth to them according to his own wisdom. And let him learn from them all the good, precious, and pure traits, which purify souls to beautify them out of their dinginess. And be more diligent to remember them, and a supernal power that you did not know will be renewed within you. And a person is obligated to think of all these remembrances always, at every hour and in the blink of an eye. And let him be careful to remember them with every breath, so that awe, fear, and shame before God — who always sees him at every time — never depart from him. Go and learn what the Torah warned the king of Israel, as it is written (Deuteronomy 17:18-19), "and he shall write for himself a copy of this Torah in a book, from before the priests, the Levites... and it shall be with him, and he shall read it all the days of his life"; and it is written (Joshua 1:8), "this book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth, and you shall meditate in it day and night"; and it says (Deuteronomy 6:6-9), "and these words, which I command you this day, shall be upon your heart. And you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up. And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. And you shall write them..."; "and it shall be to you a fringe... that you may remember..." (Numbers 15:39-40). Accordingly it is fitting to remember God at every moment. And it is written (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "let your garments always be white."
Orchot Tzadikim 19:37: See how the trait of remembrance is dear before the Omnipresent. For at the time Israel made the [Golden] Calf and were sentenced to death, and Moses said (Exodus 32:13), "remember Abraham..." (and the Lord said, "I have forgiven, as you have spoken..."). See how expansive the trait of remembrance is, for through it one remembers all the good traits, and were it not for that remembrance, everything would be forgotten and one would remain empty of everything. Therefore let a person strengthen himself in this trait, which is the strongest of all traits. And this is a great remedy for acquiring all the traits: that he accustom himself to review this book, and then he will remember all the traits and keep them; at the very least he should review it once a week. And the summary signs of the traits written at the end of the book he should review twice each day, and always examine himself as to whether he has fallen short in fulfilling the traits, until he becomes accustomed to take from every trait the good that is in it.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:38: And know that remembrance leads to action, as it is written (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall remember... and do them" — therefore strengthen yourself greatly in the trait of remembrance. And be careful to remember, for each and every commandment, for whose sake you perform it, and who is the Master of your labor.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:39: And a person must be very careful not to remember it if his fellow did him harm, and of this it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "nor bear a grudge"; rather, let him forget all hatred from his heart. But if he did harm to his fellow, let him remember it, so that he may correct what he did to him. And if he heard idle talk, he should not remember it, but should be like a sieve that catches the fine flour and lets the chaff pass through — not like a strainer that catches the sediment and lets the wine pass through.
Orchot Tzadikim 19:40: We shall explain the matter of remembering the Torah, with God's help, in the Gate of Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 20:2: Forgetfulness is a very bad trait in the matters of this world and in the matters of the World to Come. Whoever is forgetful should write down all matters between himself and his fellow so that he remember. If he borrows and lends, he should write everything down; even if he borrows a single coin from his fellow, he should write it all down, and take care not to forget. And it is fitting for a person who is important and forgetful not to borrow from people, for they are ashamed to ask him [to repay], and he forgets and does not repay, and bears the guilt. And whoever knows himself to be forgetful must be very careful to review his affairs. A parable: a certain king gave one of his attending servants a letter, and said to him: when you see that I am angry, give it to me. And the letter was written in this language: know that you are not God, but a perishable body, part of which will consume another part, and will return within itself to worms and maggots. And the king had a servant whom he commanded to stand before him whenever he ordered people struck with fiery lashes, and he would say this to him to subdue his heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 20:3: From this one learns several things: a person who is forgetful should make reminders for himself. And great fences are needed so that one not forget the Torah, as it is written (Deuteronomy 4:9), "only take heed to yourself, and guard your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen." And one must be careful not to forget the good traits.
Orchot Tzadikim 20:4: But he should make use of the trait of forgetfulness to forget the commandments he has performed. For if he takes care to remember his commandments and his good deeds, and forgets his bad deeds and his schemes, he will consider himself righteous and not do teshuvah. Rather, let him remember his transgressions, write them in a book, and read them so as to remember them all, and repent of each one and confess over them. But he should not concern himself with remembering a commandment he has performed; he should always imagine himself as though he were empty of commandments and full of transgressions. And he should forget his fellow's sins and forgive him, and forget hatred, envy, and improper thoughts from his heart. And at the time of prayer he should forget everything in the world from his heart, but let the kindness of the Blessed Lord rise in his thought, and cleave to Him with great devotion. And when he attends to his bodily needs, he should forget from his heart all words of Torah and holiness, but think about his household needs at that time, and think that he is full of filth, and by this humble his heart. In sum: for every single commandment, he should do what will keep him from forgetting it, "for the commandment is a lamp, and the Torah is light" (Proverbs 6:23).
Orchot Tzadikim 21:2: Silence and speech. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said (Avot 1:17): all my days I grew up among the Sages, and I found nothing better for the body than silence. And so King Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 17:28), "even a fool, if he keeps silent, is considered wise." And the wise man said: when I speak, it rules over me; for if I speak to a person something improper, that very utterance rules over me, and requires me to submit before him and ask his forgiveness. But when I do not speak, I rule over whether to say it or hide it. Our Sages of blessed memory said: two advocates stood before Hadrian, one arguing that speech is good, and one arguing that silence is good. The king said to the one arguing that speech is good: how do you say this? He said to him: my lord! Were it not for speech, how would kings be crowned in the world, how would ships set out to sea, how would kindness be done for the dead, how would brides be praised, how would there be commerce in the world? At once King Hadrian said to him: you have spoken well! He said to the one who argued that silence is good: how did you praise silence? At once he began to speak. Then the one who argued that speech is good came and slapped him. The king said to him: why did you slap him? He said to him: my master! I taught from my own [domain] about my own — for I taught about speech from speech. But this one came to teach from mine about his own! Therefore I slapped him. The king said to him: did not Solomon say otherwise? He did not say to sit silent like a deaf man, but said (Proverbs 10:19), "in the multitude of words, sin is not lacking, but he who restrains his lips is wise." Its meaning: one who restrains and refrains from speaking about his fellow. There is none greater than Aaron and Miriam — the well rose and gave water by the merit of Miriam, peace upon her, and clouds of glory surrounded Israel by the merit of Aaron; yet once they gave license to their mouths and spoke against Moses, they were punished at once (Numbers 12).
Orchot Tzadikim 21:3: For several matters the Divine Presence departs from Israel: because of bloodshed, idolatry, and slander. There is a story of Rabban Gamliel, who made a feast and gave his servant tongues to cook. He prepared some cooked well, and made some hard and some soft. He served the hard ones before them first, then afterward served the soft ones. He called his servant and said to him: why did you do this, serving some hard and some soft? He said to him: to let you know that everything depends on the tongue — if a person wishes, he can make it soft or hard.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:4: They said to a wise man: why do you keep so much silence? He said to them: I found speech to divide into four parts. One, entirely harmful, such as people accustomed to cursing others and speaking vulgar words. The second, harmful from one side, such as one who praises another to receive some benefit from him; and in that very praise he angers that person's enemy, and harms the one he praised in the eyes of his own enemy. The third, neither harmful nor beneficial, such as vain matters: "how such-and-such a wall was built," "and so-and-so spent this much on it," and tales of kings and officers. The fourth, entirely beneficial, such as Torah and matters dependent on it. But there are Torah sages who divide speech into five parts: the first, commanded; the second, one must be careful of it; the third, disgraceful; the fourth, beloved; the fifth, permitted. Commanded — that is, to speak words of Torah and fear of Heaven. One must be careful of — such as false testimony, vulgar speech, and gossip. Disgraceful — containing neither transgression nor benefit, like most worldly tales, such as speaking of things already past, and the customs of kings, and many matters of the world. Beloved — this is speech that praises good deeds and disparages bad deeds: to praise the deeds of the righteous, so that people's conduct improve in their eyes and they follow their ways; and to disparage the wicked, until they become disgraced and despised in people's eyes and their memory is blotted out, and people distance themselves from them and do not follow their ways. Permitted — eating, drinking, and other needs; whoever minimizes his words on this matter is praiseworthy. According to the words of the Sages, most of the world's talk has no need behind it, apart from things it is very forbidden to speak of, such as mockery, flattery, falsehood, and telling slander. Regarding these four, a separate gate should be written for each one, further on.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:5: In several places silence is good. Such as a person struck by the attribute of [strict] judgment, as Aaron did, as it is said (Leviticus 10:3), "and Aaron was silent." And if he hears people reviling him, let him be silent — and this is the great virtue: to be silent toward those who revile. Also, a person should accustom himself to silence in the privy, and this is his modesty. And this requires great diligence: to be silent in the synagogue, and refrain from speaking even words of Torah there, and how much more so other matters — all so that he can direct his heart to prayer. And if he sits among the wise, let him be silent and listen to their words; for when he is silent, he hears what he did not know, but when he speaks, he adds no knowledge. But if he is in doubt about the words of the Sages, let him ask them, for this silence is very bad. King Solomon, peace upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 3:7), "a time to be silent, and a time to speak" — sometimes speech is good, and sometimes silence is good. And the wise man said: when you cannot find a person to teach you ethical wisdom, cling to silence, lest you speak folly. And since the tongue is very light [i.e. quick to move], one must be very careful to make the tongue heavy, to guard it from speaking. Most words are like a heavy burden. And the heaviness of much speech is greater than the heaviness of much silence. And if he hears his fellow speaking, let him remain silent until he finishes his words, for "he who answers a matter before he hears it, it is folly and shame to him" (Proverbs 18:13).
Orchot Tzadikim 21:6: Whoever is accustomed to silence is saved from several transgressions: from flattery, from mockery, from slander, from lies and insults. For when a person reviles and insults him, if he answers back, the other will double his insults. And so the wise man said: I hear an evil word, and I remain silent. They said to him: why? He said to them: if I were to reply and answer back to those who revile me, I fear I would hear other insults harsher than the first. And he said: when a fool argues with a wise man, and the wise man remains silent, this is a great retort to the fool, for the fool is pained by the wise man's silence more than if he had answered him. And of this it is said (Proverbs 26:4), "answer not a fool according to his folly."
Orchot Tzadikim 21:7: Also: a person can reveal secrets to him, since he is not accustomed to much talk, he will not reveal them. Also, he is not accustomed to gossip. Of this it is said (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue." For a person does more with his tongue than with his sword: for a person standing here can hand over his fellow, far away from him, to death, but the sword kills only at close range. Therefore two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and one mouth were created in a person, to teach that he should minimize his speech. Silence is good for the wise, how much more so for fools. A fence for wisdom is silence (Avot 3:13). The remedy for everything is silence (Megillah 18a).
Orchot Tzadikim 21:8: And sometimes silence is bad, as it is written (Proverbs 26:5), "answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes." In matters of Torah: if he sees fools mocking the words of the wise, he should answer them to correct their error, so that they not be wise in their own eyes. If he sees a person committing a transgression, he should protest with his hand and rebuke him. And Solomon already said (Proverbs 15:1), "a soft answer turns away wrath"; "and a gentle tongue breaks a bone" (ibid. 25:15). Therefore a person should accustom himself to have gentle words, and not be accustomed to harsh words. And be careful with your tongue to guard it like the pupil of the eye, for "the mouth of a fool is his own ruin, and his lips are the snare of his soul" (ibid. 18:7); and it is written (ibid. 21:23), "whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles"; and it is said (Job 13:5), "oh that you would altogether hold your peace, and it would be your wisdom." And if you sit with understanding, it is better that people say to you, "speak! why are you so silent?" than that you speak and your words become a burden to them, so they say to you, "be silent!"
Orchot Tzadikim 21:9: And he should be careful not to shame a person or cause him grief with his words. If he sits near a person who has a blemish on his body that he is ashamed of, or whose children or wife have a blemish he is ashamed of, or whose family has a flaw, he should be careful not to speak of that blemish or that flaw, even if he does not speak of him but speaks of another man who has this same flaw, since the first man will always suppose he is being spoken of and will be ashamed.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:10: If a person did something disgraceful, and then turned back from it and did teshuvah, one should be careful not to speak of that deed in front of him, and not even say to him, even in jest, "how did you do such a thing, and were not careful about it, when you should have done it a different way!" Or if a person tells you something you already know, remain silent until he finishes speaking, for perhaps he will tell you something new that you did not know at first; also, he derives pleasure from telling you something. And even if you know he will tell you nothing new, remain silent until he finishes.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:11: Two people who had a quarrel with one another, and afterward were reconciled — neither of them should speak and say, "you did such-and-such to me, and therefore I did such-and-such to you," even if he has no intention of returning to the dispute. For because he says to him, "you did such-and-such to me," his fellow will answer him, "on the contrary, the wrongdoing was yours," and through this they will arouse the quarrel again. And even if the quarrel is not aroused again, he will have shamed him for his wrongdoing.
Orchot Tzadikim 21:12: There is one who sits before a wise man and is silent, and has reward for it, such as one who intends to listen. And there is one who is silent and has a transgression for it, such as one who thinks: "why should I speak before him, since he does not know how to answer me properly? Surely he knows nothing compared to me." And he must be very careful about what our Sages of blessed memory said (Avot 5:7): seven traits are in the uncultivated person, and seven in the wise man: the wise man does not speak before one greater than he in wisdom or in number; he does not interrupt his fellow's words; he is not hasty to answer; he asks according to the matter and answers according to the law; he speaks of the first point first and the last point last; and regarding what he has not heard, he says, "I have not heard," and he acknowledges the truth. And the opposite of these traits are in the uncultivated person.
